title: Linux Command Line & Networking
subtitle: Work confidently in the shell and understand how networks connect computers.
outcomes: Navigate files and directories from the command line
Combine commands with pipes and filters
Automate tasks with loops and shell scripts
Explain key networking and network-security concepts

toc.text: General Syntax of a Shell Command
Step one: see where we are and what we already have
Operations with multiple files and directories
Using wildcards for accessing multiple files at once
What is encryption at rest and in transit?
How does network segmentation help implement zero trust?

pool.q: What is a shell?
options: A program whose primary purpose is to read commands and run other programs
The physical case of a computer
pool.explain: The shell is the command-line interface between you and the operating system.
pool.evidence: A shell is a program whose primary purpose is to read commands and run other programs.

pool.q: What does a command-line interface (CLI) let users do?
options: Interact with a computer by reading and writing text
pool.explain: Text commands are easy to repeat, combine and automate.
pool.evidence: A command-line interface (CLI) allows users to interact with a computer by reading and writing text.

pool.q: What is your current working directory?
options: The one place you are in at any moment while using the shell
The folder where the shell program is installed
The root of the file system
pool.explain: Relative paths are interpreted from the current working directory (see pwd).
pool.evidence: at any time while we are using the shell, we are in exactly one place called our current working directory

pool.q: Which part of the operating system manages files and directories?
pool.explain: The shell is one way of interacting with it.
pool.evidence: The part of the operating system responsible for managing files and directories is called the file system

pool.q: What does the command pwd stand for?
pool.explain: It shows where you are in the file system.
pool.evidence: running a command called pwd (which stands for 'print working directory')

pool.q: How is an absolute path written?
options: As the full path from the root directory, starting with a slash
pool.explain: Relative paths start from your current working directory instead.
pool.evidence: it is possible to specify the absolute path to a directory by including its entire path from the root directory, which is indicated by a leading slash

pool.q: What does ls -t do?
options: Lists items by time of last change instead of alphabetically
pool.explain: ls has many options, and you can combine them.
pool.evidence: The command ls -t lists items by time of last change instead of alphabetically.

pool.q: What is the difference between cd .. and cd -?
options: cd .. goes up one level; cd - goes back to the previous directory
They do exactly the same thing
pool.explain: Up means the parent directory; back means where you were before.
pool.evidence: the former brings you up

pool.q: Why is it better to avoid spaces in the names of files and directories?
options: Spaces are not allowed by any operating system
Spaces are used to separate arguments on the command line
pool.explain: Use hyphens or underscores instead, e.g. north-pacific-gyre.
pool.evidence: since spaces are used to separate arguments on the command line it is better to avoid them in names of files and directories.

pool.q: Are the files you see in the shell different from those in a file explorer?
options: Yes, the shell has its own copies
No — they are the same files, accessed in two ways
pool.explain: Changes in one show up in the other.
pool.evidence: While the shell and the file explorer are two different ways of interacting with the files, the files and directories themselves are the same.

pool.q: Does mv ask before overwriting an existing file?
pool.explain: Be careful: mv can silently replace a file.
pool.evidence: By default, mv will not ask for confirmation before overwriting files.

pool.q: Can files deleted with rm always be recovered?
options: No — there's no guarantee, as the disk space may be reused immediately
pool.explain: The shell has no recycle bin.
pool.evidence: since the computer may recycle the file's disk space right away

pool.q: What does rm -i do?
options: Asks for confirmation before every removal
pool.explain: It's a safer way to delete files.
pool.evidence: The -i option will prompt before (every) removal

pool.q: When you use wildcards such as *.txt, what do commands like ls actually receive?
options: The list of matching file names, not the wildcard itself
pool.explain: The shell expands wildcards before running the command.
pool.evidence: commands like wc and ls see the lists of file names matching these expressions, but not the wildcards themselves

pool.q: A command is waiting for input and seems stuck. How do you get out?
pool.explain: Ctrl + C interrupts the running program.
pool.evidence: you can escape out of this state by holding down the control key ( Ctrl ) and pressing the letter C once

pool.q: Why does wc -l *.pdb > lengths.txt print nothing on screen?
options: Its output was redirected into lengths.txt
pool.explain: > sends output to a file instead of the screen.
pool.evidence: This command prints no screen output, because everything that wc would have printed has gone into the file lengths.txt instead.

pool.q: What does sort -n do?
pool.explain: Without -n, 10 sorts before 2.
pool.evidence: The -n option specifies a numerical rather than an alphanumerical sort.

pool.q: Is it safe to redirect a command's output into the same file it is reading?
options: No — it's a very bad idea
pool.explain: The file can be emptied before the command reads it.
pool.evidence: It's a very bad idea to try redirecting the output of a command that operates on a file to the same file.

pool.q: What problem do pipes solve compared with saving intermediate files?
options: Intermediate files make it hard to follow what's going on
pool.explain: A pipe sends one command's output straight into the next.
pool.evidence: those intermediate files make it hard to follow what's going on

pool.q: What do loops let you do in the shell?
options: Repeat a command or set of commands for each item in a list
pool.explain: for filename in *.dat; do …; done applies the same steps to every file.
pool.evidence: Loops are a programming construct which allow us to repeat a command or set of commands for each item in a list.

pool.q: What is each run of a loop called?
pool.explain: Each iteration assigns the next item in the list to the loop variable.
pool.evidence: Each time the loop runs (called an iteration)

pool.q: In a shell for loop, which word marks the end of the loop?
pool.explain: The word do marks the start of the commands to repeat.
pool.evidence: The word "done" indicates the end of a loop

pool.q: How do you loop over file names that contain spaces?
options: Put quotes around them and around the loop variable
Use a backslash at the end of the line
pool.explain: Spaces otherwise split one name into two items.
pool.evidence: If one of those elements contains a space character, we need to surround it with quotes, and do the same thing to our loop variable.

pool.q: How do you use the value of a loop variable inside the loop?
options: Prefix its name with a dollar sign
pool.explain: Without $, the shell treats it as plain text.
pool.evidence: expanding the loop variable name because we have prefixed it with a dollar sign

pool.q: What is a shell script?
options: A set of commands saved in a file — really a small program
A log of commands you typed yesterday
pool.explain: Saving repeated commands lets you re-run a whole workflow with a single command.
pool.evidence: a bunch of commands saved in a file is usually called a shell script

pool.q: When editing shell scripts, which kind of editor should you use?
options: A plain text editor, or save files as plain text
pool.explain: Word processors add formatting characters that break scripts.
pool.evidence: When editing programs, therefore, you must either use a plain text editor or be careful to save files as plain text.

pool.q: Why save frequently repeated commands in a file?
options: So you can re-run them all later with a single command
To hide them from other users
pool.explain: Such a file is a shell script — a small program.
pool.evidence: We are going to take the commands we repeat frequently and save them in files so that we can re-run all those operations again later by typing a single command.

pool.q: Inside a shell script, what does $1 mean?
options: The first filename or other argument on the command line
The first line of the file
pool.explain: It makes scripts work on any file you pass in.
pool.evidence: means 'the first filename (or other argument) on the command line'

pool.q: What does the special variable $@ mean in a script?
options: All the command-line arguments passed to the script
pool.explain: Put it in double quotes to handle names with spaces.
pool.evidence: which means, 'All of the command-line arguments to the shell script'

pool.q: Which command finds files and directories whose names match simple patterns?
pool.explain: grep searches inside files for lines that match; find searches for the files themselves.
pool.evidence: Use find to find files and directories whose names match simple patterns.

pool.q: What does grep do?
options: Finds and prints lines in files that match a pattern
pool.explain: find, by contrast, finds files and directories.
pool.evidence: grep finds and prints lines in files that match a pattern

pool.q: Searching for 'The' also matched the word 'Thesis'. Why?
options: grep matches the pattern inside larger words unless told otherwise
pool.explain: Options can restrict matches to whole words.
pool.evidence: one of which contained our search pattern within a larger word, 'Thesis'

pool.q: Which grep option limits matches to whole words?
pool.explain: -n numbers matching lines; -i ignores case.
pool.evidence: we can give grep the -w option

pool.q: Which grep option makes a search case-insensitive?
pool.explain: Then 'The' and 'the' both match.
pool.evidence: use the option -i to make our search case-insensitive

pool.q: When is UDP a suitable protocol?
options: When every packet must arrive in order
When speed and efficiency matter more than guaranteed delivery
pool.explain: Streaming, gaming and DNS lookups prefer speed; TCP guarantees delivery.
pool.evidence: UDP is suitable for applications where speed and efficiency are more important than guaranteed delivery

pool.q: When is TCP the right protocol?
options: When speed matters more than delivery
When applications need reliable, ordered delivery and accurate data
pool.explain: UDP suits streaming and gaming, where speed matters more than guaranteed delivery.
pool.evidence: TCP prioritizes reliability and ordered delivery, making it suitable for applications that require data accuracy

pool.q: Why is network segmentation used?
options: To reduce the number of IP addresses
To make the network easier to cable
To contain the impact of breaches and limit attackers' lateral movement
pool.explain: Isolated segments with strict access policies stop an intruder spreading.
pool.evidence: Network segmentation is used to improve security by containing the impact of potential breaches and limiting lateral movement for attackers within the network.

pool.q: How does network segmentation support identity-based access control?
options: It removes the need for logins
Users and devices are authenticated and authorised before reaching specific segments
It gives every user full access
pool.explain: Access between segments follows security policies.
pool.evidence: Network segmentation also aids in enforcing identity-based access controls, where users and devices are thoroughly authenticated and authorized before accessing specific segments.

pool.q: What do cloud security groups let organisations define?
options: Rules for which types of traffic are allowed and denied
pool.explain: They add a layer of defence to cloud deployments.
pool.evidence: Security groups allow organizations to define rules that determine which types of traffic are allowed and denied

pool.q: What does the HTTPS guidance require for your service, including its APIs?
options: It must only be accessible through secure connections
It must allow plain HTTP for older browsers
It must use a separate domain for each page
It must block all mobile devices
pool.explain: Encryption in transit stops information being intercepted or modified.
pool.evidence: you must make sure your service (including APIs ) is only accessible through secure connections.
